title: Numbers That Change When Each Digit Turns
statement:
Picture a number drawn on a digital display. Turn every digit on its own half a circle, keeping the digits in their places. Then:

  • 0, 1 and 8 look the same;
  • 2 and 5 turn into each other, and so do 6 and 9;
  • 3, 4 and 7 turn into something that is not a digit.

A number is good if every digit still reads as a digit after turning, and the resulting number is different from the original. Return how many integers in [1, n] are good.

examples.why: 2, 5, 6 and 9 change. 1, 8 and 10 turn into themselves; 3, 4 and 7 break.
Only 2, 5 and 6. The 7 is not valid at all.

hints: Checking every number up to 10⁹ digit by digit is too slow. Count instead of listing.
Good = (all digits from {0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9}) minus (all digits from {0, 1, 8}). The second group turns into itself, so it is exactly the part that does not change.

Counting numbers ≤ n whose digits all come from a set S: walk n's digits from the left. At each position, every allowed digit smaller than n's digit lets the rest be anything from S, which is |S|^(remaining) numbers. Stop if n's own digit is not in S.

explain.intuition:
A number is valid if all its digits are in {0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9}, and it stays the same exactly when all its digits are in {0, 1, 8}. So the good numbers are "valid" minus "unchanged", and both are the same kind of count: how many numbers up to n use only digits from a given set.

That count has a classic left-to-right form. Pad numbers with leading zeros to the length of n. At the first position where a number goes below n, it picks a smaller allowed digit, and every later position is free: |S|^remaining choices. Sum that over positions while n's own prefix stays allowed, and add 1 if all of n's digits are allowed. Zero is counted by both sets, so it cancels in the subtraction.
steps: Write countUpTo(n, S): numbers in [0, n] whose digits are all in S.
Walk the digits d of n from the left with rest digits after it. Add (allowed digits < d) · |S|^rest.
If d is not in S, return the sum so far. If you finish all digits, add 1 for n itself.
pitfalls: Treating the number as turned around as a whole, reversing the digit order. Each digit turns in place.
Counting numbers with only 0, 1 and 8 as good. They are valid but unchanged.
Forgetting to stop once n's own digit is not allowed: later positions can no longer follow n's prefix.

solutions.title: Check every number
solutions.idea: For each number from 1 to n, look at its digits: reject on 3, 4 or 7, accept if any digit is 2, 5, 6 or 9.

solutions.title: Count by digit sets
solutions.idea: Numbers using only valid digits minus numbers using only 0, 1, 8. Each count walks n's digits once.

followups: Count the numbers in [lo, hi] instead of [1, n].
Count the numbers that read as a different valid number when the whole display is turned upside down, so the digit order reverses too.
